title: N-Queens
description: Place n queens on an n×n board so no two attack each other, using backtracking with column and diagonal sets.

data.text: Place `n` queens on an `n × n` chessboard so that no two queens attack each other — no two on the same row, column, or diagonal. Return all distinct solutions. Each solution is the list of column indices, one per row.

**Input:** `n = 4`

**Output:** `[[1, 3, 0, 2], [2, 0, 3, 1]]`

**Explanation:** Two ways to place four queens. For `n = 8` there are 92, and the count grows roughly as `n! / (c^n)`.

Process one row at a time. In each row try every column that is not already attacked, place a queen, recurse to the next row, then remove the queen and try the next column. A row can never contain two queens, so you never need to check the row condition — that is enforced by the recursion depth.

data.title: Backtracking with attack sets — O(n!) with pruning
data.content: Three sets track columns and both diagonal directions.

data.title: The diagonal identity is the whole trick
data.text: Every square on a down-right diagonal has the same `row + col`, and every square on an up-right diagonal has the same `row - col`. Testing those two integers replaces an O(n) scan along each diagonal with two O(1) set lookups.

data.title: Undo state before continuing, not after the loop
data.text: The three removals must happen immediately after the recursive call, inside the loop. If you defer them until after the loop, the state is still polluted when you try the next column and valid placements get pruned away.

data.caption: Row by row, each column is either pruned by an attack set or recursed into; the sets are restored on the way back up.

data.title: Complete solution
data.content: N-Queens is the canonical 'constraint satisfaction by backtracking' problem. The general recipe applies to Sudoku, scheduling with conflicts, and configuration problems: represent partial state, find a cheap validity predicate, prune early, and always restore state on the way back up.
